abstract: Streaming video understanding requires models to repeatedly decide whether to respond or continue observing. Recently, Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) has been applied to this setting, with existing approaches emphasizing reward design while retaining a single trajectory-level advantage across turns. Such shared credit can reinforce redundant replies after earlier successes and discourage useful follow-ups after earlier failures. We propose TurnWise, a turn-level GRPO framework that aligns learning with individual streaming decisions. TurnWise addresses the mismatch between trajectory-level feedback and turn-level interaction, promoting informative responses and reducing redundancy. Specifically, turn-level credit assignment uses silence-completed prefix scoring to construct group-relative advantages from each decision’s remaining return, separating its learning signal from earlier rewards. Turn-mean policy optimization averages token losses within each turn and then across turns, giving response and waiting decisions equal weight regardless of output length. These complementary designs improve streaming policy learning without a learned critic or additional rollouts. Extensive experiments show our method outperforms prior RL approaches for streaming video understanding.

sections.body: The introduction argues that streaming video models make repeated respond-or-wait decisions, and that GRPO's single trajectory-level advantage can credit a redundant reply after an earlier success. It identifies a granularity mismatch: shared advantages obscure later decisions, and token-mean loss aggregation makes each turn's weight depend on response length. TurnWise combines silence-completed prefix scoring, which gives turn-specific remaining-return advantages, with turn-mean loss aggregation. The method needs no learned critic and no additional rollouts. The stated evidence is the best aggregate scores on ProactiveVQA, OVO-Timing and StreamingBench with both Qwen backbones.
sections.heading: Introduction
sections.headline: Shared trajectory-level advantages misassign credit to redundant replies and useful follow-ups in streaming video reinforcement learning.

sections.body: This section places the work among streaming video systems, including MMDuet, ThinkStream, StreamBridge and Streamo, and among reinforcement learning methods for video such as Video-R1 and VideoChat-R1. It notes that MMDuet2, ThinkStream and StreamPro improve reward design or combine turn-level and trajectory-level rewards. The authors state that these approaches still derive a shared advantage from the aggregated reward. The section frames the paper's contribution as how feedback is assigned and weighted across decisions.
sections.heading: Related Work
sections.headline: Prior streaming video methods use trajectory-level GRPO, which broadcasts one advantage across all decision turns.

sections.body: The method scores each trajectory prefix $U_{i,t}$ by keeping its first $t$ actions and setting all later turns to silence. The remaining return $F_{i,t}=R_{i}-U_{i,t-1}$ excludes rewards accrued earlier. Subtracting the group average of accrued reward gives a turn-specific advantage, clipped to $\pm 5$ in experiments. An interpolation strength $\alpha$ is warmed up from 0 to 1 over the first 10% of updates. The reward is the PAUC-based trajectory score from MMDuet2, which combines response quality and timing with repetition, out-of-window and prefix penalties. Turn-mean aggregation averages token losses within each turn and then across turns, so each decision receives weight $1/T_i$. The advantages are computed from existing rollout evaluations, without a learned critic or extra rollouts.
sections.heading: Methodology
sections.headline: Silence-completed prefix scores give each turn a remaining-return advantage, and turn-mean averaging weights every turn equally.

sections.body: Qwen2.5-VL-3B and Qwen3-VL-4B are first fine-tuned on a corpus of 100,874 valid instruction examples, then trained with GRPO-style reinforcement learning on 3,983 streaming instances. Each instance uses $G=4$ rollouts, batch size 8, and AdamW at learning rate $10^{-6}$ for one epoch, with no KL or entropy regularization. Training trajectories are judged by gpt-oss-20b. Evaluation uses ProactiveVQA with 300 instances, OVO-Timing with Timing F1 within $\pm 2$ seconds, and StreamingBench. Baselines are supervised fine-tuned models, MMDuet2, ThinkStream and StreamPro, all run in the same streaming GRPO framework.
sections.heading: Experiments
sections.headline: Experiments compare TurnWise with fine-tuned and reinforcement-learning baselines on three streaming benchmarks using two Qwen backbones.

sections.body: TurnWise achieves the best aggregate scores on all three benchmarks with both backbones. On Qwen2.5-VL-3B it exceeds the strongest non-TurnWise result by 3.96 on ProactiveVQA, 3.87 on OVO-Timing and 0.69 on StreamingBench. Combining turn-level credit with turn-mean aggregation reduces repetition from 15.53 to 5.98 relative to credit-only optimization, and raises Timing F1 by 2.96 points. Full correction with $\alpha=1$ is best on all four metrics in the 3B ablation. Mean reward rises from 0.657 to 0.711 over the final 50 updates under turn-mean aggregation.
sections.heading: Results and Discussions
sections.headline: TurnWise posts the best aggregate scores on all three benchmarks, reaching 43.56 on ProactiveVQA with the 3B backbone.

sections.body: The conclusion restates that silence-completed prefix references remove previously accrued rewards from later-turn credit. It also states that turn-mean aggregation gives response and waiting decisions equal weight, without a learned critic or additional rollouts. It reports the best aggregate results on all three benchmarks across two Qwen backbones. It presents the component analyses as support for higher-quality, better-timed and more selective responses. The section adds no new numerical results.
sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.headline: Turn-level credit without a critic supports higher-quality, better-timed and more selective streaming responses.

sections.body: The appendix defines silence-completed prefix scores with a fixed scoring context, so the all-silent reference $U_{0}$ is shared across the group. Telescoping shows that accrued reward $C_{i,t-1}$ plus remaining return $F_{i,t}$ equals $R_{i}-U_{0}$. Centering the remaining return gives the group-relative correction, and the derivation holds for non-additive scorers such as ratio-based repetition penalties. It gives the interpolation over $\alpha$ and the warm-up over the first 10% of updates. It also specifies the dual-clipping safeguard with $c=3$, applied to generated action tokens with turn-mean aggregation.
sections.heading: Appendix
sections.headline: The appendix derives the telescoping decomposition, the group-relative correction, the interpolation and warm-up schedule, and the dual-clipping loss.
